claims.text: The initial FeNiCrCoCu coating is an FCC solid solution.
The initial coating has low dislocation density and no amorphous regions.
Above 900 K, plasticity transitions from dislocation-mediated deformation to thermally activated amorphization.
Stacking-fault annihilation and an inability to sustain dislocation networks drive the high-temperature transition.
Stacking faults are annihilated and dislocation starvation occurs at 600 K.
Dislocation starvation at 600 K causes elastic stiffening.
Above 900 K, thermal activation overcomes the Peierls barrier and lattice-distortion energy, causing rapid lattice disorder.
High-temperature stacking-fault annihilation and dislocation starvation prevent stable dislocation networks from forming.
Loss of stable dislocation networks triggers an amorphous-like state in the indentation zone.
The resulting amorphous regions have lower shear resistance than the crystalline material.
The amorphous regions have greater adhesion to the indenter.
Lower shear resistance and increased adhesion in amorphous regions cause the friction-coefficient spike.
Loss of crystalline strain-hardening mechanisms causes the sharp reduction in wear resistance.
Hardness increases slightly at 600 K because of dislocation starvation.
Hardness declines sharply above 900 K.
The friction coefficient spikes at 900 K and 1200 K in correlation with amorphization.
HCP atom count transiently increases at 600 K because of twinning.
HCP atom count decreases by 1200 K as the material becomes amorphous.
Dislocation line length peaks at 600 K.
Dislocation line length decays to near zero at 1200 K.

contradictions.description: The mediator asserts dislocation starvation at 600 K, whereas the predicted outcome asserts that dislocation line length peaks at 600 K. Without distinguishing mobile from stored dislocations or specifying a temporal sequence, these descriptions conflict.

Stacking-fault annihilation is assigned to 600 K, but HCP content is also predicted to increase at 600 K because of twinning, which ordinarily generates or preserves fault-related HCP signatures. No competing-rate explanation is provided.

The mechanism says amorphization causes the friction spike, so successfully suppressing amorphization should eliminate the spike and support the mechanism. The falsification rule instead states that absence of a spike when amorphization is suppressed would falsify the hypothesis, reversing the causal test.

Amorphization is described as occurring above 900 K, while the predicted friction spike is attributed to amorphization at 900 K itself. The treatment of 900 K as either below or within the onset regime is inconsistent.
